core_condition: at least one measured effect recorded in observed_effects from Ventora telemetry or public corpora

evidence.rationale: A well-formalised theory with computational validation but a narrow empirical base. Pirolli & Card (1999) derived information foraging from optimal foraging theory and formalised information scent; earlier work established the framework in information-access environments (1995); Pirolli's 2007 monograph consolidates it. SNIF-ACT provides computational models predicting user navigation on the web, and applied work — the scent-of-a-site analyses and scented-widget studies — manipulates scent directly and measures navigation outcomes. Scored 2 rather than 3 because validation is concentrated in hypertext search and browse tasks with limited datasets, and because the theory's predictive machinery has not been extensively tested against modern app, feed and mobile interaction.

product_applicability.rationale: Immediately implementable and consequential: specific destination-predicting labels in user vocabulary, and preview cues that let a path be assessed before it is entered. Reference: search snippets as an explicit scent mechanism, well-labelled settings and documentation, counts and previews in list interfaces. Directly relevant wherever a generated product has more than one path.

measurability.rationale: Unusually good for this node: navigation success rate, drop-off by step, exploration rate and time-to-first-value are all reachable in our telemetry and map closely to what the theory predicts. Label changes are also cleanly A/B-testable, which makes this the most directly testable perception mechanism we have.

orthogonality.rationale: Clear boundaries with neighbours: SC-17 describes how a view is sampled, IF-18 how the resulting cues drive path choice; CG-05 creates an information gap deliberately, IF-18 governs the search for one. Enabled by CL-14 as an economising strategy but not reducible to it.

safety.rationale: Low intrinsic hazard — accurate, predictive labelling serves users by definition. Two misuse vectors are blocked: false scent (labels or previews promising what the destination does not deliver, which is the mechanism underlying clickbait and misleading links), and scent suppression on exit paths — deliberately vague cancellation, unsubscribe and downgrade labelling, which is a specifically regulated dark pattern under click-to-cancel and DSA rules. Both boundaries are sharp and testable.

dissent: Two limitations discipline the claim, plus one honest note about how thin this corpus was before correction. (1) Domain narrowness: foraging theory was developed and validated for goal-directed information seeking in hypertext — searching and browsing toward a known want. Much modern product interaction is not goal-directed in that sense (feeds, ambient consumption, exploratory use), and it is not established that scent-following describes behaviour there. We claim the mechanism where the user is looking for something, and not as a general model of interface behaviour. (2) Model validation: the computational models (SNIF-ACT and successors) are validated against relatively small datasets and specific site structures; their predictive accuracy in the studied contexts does not license treating scent as a quantifiable design parameter. We use the qualitative claim — specific predictive cues sustain pursuit, generic cues cause abandonment — and not any numerical scent optimisation. (3) Corpus note: the first harvest for this mechanism was dominated by ecological foraging and economics search-cost literature through terminological collision, and was discarded; the corrected harvest is on-topic and contains the canon, but the review-anchor filter again found no qualifying topical review, so coverage rests on the resolved pin plus term breadth.

Verdict INCUBATING; CORE strictly on a measured effect — and note this is the perception mechanism most likely to produce a clean one, since label specificity is directly A/B-testable.
